title: DeepSeek splits V4-Flash into a floating name and a pinned id by H1 2027
body:
DeepSeek took V4-Flash out of preview on Friday, July 31, and how it did that carries more information than the benchmark table does. The 0731 build went behind the same `deepseek-v4-flash` API name the preview had used, so a caller who changed nothing got a different checkpoint on the next request. The architecture is what stayed put: 284B total parameters with 13B active per token, one shared expert plus 256 routed experts per layer with six firing per token, and a one-million-token context, identical across the two builds. The Hugging Face repository reports 304B because it carries a DSpark speculative-decoding draft module on top of that 284B base, and the weights are MIT-licensed. What moved is the post-training pass, re-run on agent and coding data, and DeepSeek's own before-and-after columns put Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 82.7 against the preview's 61.8, NL2Repo at 54.2 against 39.4, Cybergym at 76.7 against 38.7, DeepSWE at 54.4 against 7.3 and Toolathlon-Verified at 70.3 against 49.7 — benchmark scores on DeepSeek's own scale, vendor-reported on a harness nobody outside DeepSeek has run. The price did not move at all: $0.14 per million input tokens on a cache miss and $0.28 per million output tokens, the preview's published rates carried straight over.

Hold those two facts together and a signal goes missing. When a hosted API changes the artifact behind a name, the customer usually finds out through the bill — a new checkpoint arrives with a new rate card, and someone in finance notices before anyone in engineering does. DeepSeek held $0.14 and $0.28 flat across a build its own table says is 20.9 points better on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 47.1 points better on DeepSWE than the DeepSeek-V4-Flash preview it replaced, and in holding them flat it removed the one channel through which a substitution announces itself to a customer who was not reading release notes. The `deepseek-v4-flash` string written against the preview now returns something else, on an identical invoice. That is a competitive signal on purpose: the buyer gets the improvement without a price rise, which is a hard thing to answer for any vendor that funds new checkpoints by re-pricing them. It is also a disclosure gap, and both halves come out of one decision. The release leans hard into the first half — DeepSeek claims the smaller DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 now beats the larger DeepSeek-V4-Pro preview on every agentic benchmark it published, a comparison DeepSeek drew itself, against a build that is itself still in preview — and says nothing about the second.

The people this lands on are the ones who cannot re-qualify a model on a vendor's schedule. A checkpoint re-tuned on agent and coding data, tuned for Codex, speaking the Responses API natively and exposing low, high and max reasoning effort with a 384K output ceiling at the top two settings, is a different thing to hold a regression suite against than the preview build was: better on the five published benchmarks and differently behaved everywhere those five are silent. Anyone who signed off the preview for a production agent now holds a sign-off describing an artifact their API key can no longer reach. The convention the rest of the hosted-inference market settled on for exactly this problem is two addresses for one model — a floating alias for callers who want whatever is newest, and a dated, immutable id for callers who need tomorrow to return what today returned. DeepSeek publishes one address.

The prediction is that it publishes two. By the end of H1 2027, DeepSeek's own API documentation lists a version-identified model id for V4-Flash: a distinct string a caller passes in the model field, documented as continuing to serve one specific checkpoint, offered alongside the floating `deepseek-v4-flash` name and carrying no announced shutdown date. DeepSeek's own model and pricing documentation settles this and nothing else does. A temporary comparison endpoint published with an expiry, so customers can diff the old build against the new one for a few weeks, does not count — that is the cheap version of this move and the opposite of a pin. The `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` name on the Hugging Face weights repository does not count either: the weights artifact has carried a date from the start, and the claim here is about what the API accepts, not about what the download is called. A pinned route sold by a third-party host or gateway serving the MIT-licensed weights does not count, because the question is what the first-party endpoint promises. Self-hosting does not count, for the same reason.

The strongest argument against all of this is the licence. MIT weights mean DeepSeek's answer to a customer who needs a frozen checkpoint is already written and costs DeepSeek nothing: download the build you qualified and serve it yourself. A vendor that offers a pinned endpoint instead has to keep older weights resident on hardware that could be serving the current model, which is margin spent on customers who by definition are not buying the improvement, and a vendor that has open-sourced the weights has externalised that cost permanently and can defend never taking it back. The second argument is that one name per model is a product choice rather than an omission — a short model list is part of what DeepSeek sells against the sprawling menus of the metered vendors, and version strings are precisely the surface area those vendors now spend documentation budget managing. The third is retirement: if the earlier build stops being served at all, there is nothing for a second address to point at, and the prediction fails without anyone having decided anything. What cuts the other way is narrow but real. Holding the price flat spent the lever DeepSeek would otherwise use to charge for a pin, which leaves publishing one as the cheapest thing it can hand a customer who has just worked out that the name is not the artifact.

reasoning.because: The 0731 build went behind the same deepseek-v4-flash name at the preview's unchanged prices
reasoning.given: Hosted-API convention is two addresses per model: a floating alias and a dated, pinned one
reasoning.so_that: DeepSeek publishes a version-identified V4-Flash model id beside the floating name, with no expiry date attached
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; in DeepSeek's own API documentation, not a third-party gateway
reasoning.plain_language: DeepSeek swapped in a better model under the same name and price. Soon it will also offer a version you can lock.

summary: DeepSeek took V4-Flash out of preview by putting the 0731 build behind the same deepseek-v4-flash API name, at the preview's unchanged prices. Callers were re-based to a different checkpoint with no signal on the invoice. Expect a version-identified model id beside the floating name by H1 2027.
